title: Rights of the Minority Shareholder to the Corporate Dividend

items.abstract: <jats:p>Minority shareholder activism (MSA) on online interactive platforms is a new form of corporate governance in China. This paper investigates whether and how dividend-related MSA affects corporate dividend policies. We find listed firms are more likely to pay dividends and raise payout ratios with MSA. Our baseline findings are robust to a variety of robustness checks. We establish a causal relationship between MSA and future dividend payouts, with both instrumental variable approach and PSM-DID approach, and we provide evidence to show the increasing effect of MSA can be explained by exit threat and voting attendance. Our focused MSA complements the formal voting rights of minority shareholders and overcomes the absence of institutional investor monitoring. Overall, our findings suggest that minority shareholders can effectively monitor management when they are empowered with voice in the age of information.</jats:p>
title: Minority Shareholder Activism and Corporate Dividend Policy: Evidence From China

items.abstract: <jats:p>Grounded in agency theory, this study explores agency costs as a determinant of dividend policy. Specifically, we examine how dividends are related to the strength of shareholder rights. The evidence reveals an inverse association between dividend payouts and shareholder rights, indicating that firms pay higher dividends where shareholder rights are more suppressed. This evidence is consistent with the substitution hypothesis (La Porta et al., 2000), which contends that firms with weak shareholder rights need to establish a reputation for not exploiting shareholders. As a result, these firms pay dividends more generously than do firms with strong shareholder rights. In other words, dividends substitute for shareholder rights. Finally, there is evidence that regulation influences the association between dividends and shareholder rights.</jats:p>
title: Dividend Policy, Shareholder Rights, and Corporate Governance

Related Party Transactions and Minority Shareholder Rights

items.abstract: <jats:p>Corporate mergers and acquisitions can improve capital efficiency, facilitate the reallocation of corporate resources, and strengthen enterprise groups, but their decision-making structures also create acute risks for minority shareholders. Control transactions may allow incumbent controlling shareholders, prospective controllers, and management to exploit informational, voting, and bargaining advantages. Corporate mergers may likewise alter minority shareholders’ investment expectations without their effective consent. This Article develops a minorityshareholder-protection framework for M&amp;A under Chinese company and securities law. It argues for stronger fiduciary duties of controlling shareholders, prospective acquirers, directors, supervisors, and senior executives; robust disclosure and equal-treatment rules in takeovers; meaningful minority participation in merger decisionmaking; judicial review of defective resolutions and invalid merger agreements; active use of shareholder derivative litigation; and effective appraisal rights for dissenting shareholders. It further contends that the governance of hostile takeovers should be grounded in management neutrality, shareholder sovereignty, corporate social responsibility, and strict review of anti-takeover measures. The appropriate legal orientation is neither hostility to M&amp;A nor laissez-faire deference to control: law should encourage efficient combinations while rigorously regulating abuses, protect equality while moderately favoring vulnerable minority shareholders, and preserve a principled boundary against opportunistic claims by minority investors.</jats:p>
title: Protecting Minority Shareholder Rights in Corporate Mergers and Acquisitions
IV. Weak Shareholder Rights? – A Case Study of Cevian Capital’s Investment in Demag Cranes AG

items.abstract: <jats:p>During the last few years minority shareholders have suffered many shocks. Their rights and options were compromised. New legal and regulatory initiatives have failed to establish stability and trust on the mechanisms and contracts that are essential for organizational and market stability. The paper cites the basic rights of minority shareholders and analyzes the feasibility of their protection and enforcement. Minority shareholders are, in essence, without any choices or the choices that they have to rely on are the will and faculty of the dominant group (managers in the case of the Anglo-Saxon countries and major shareholders in Continental Europe countries).</jats:p>
title: Minority Shareholder Choices and Rights in the New Market Environment

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper investigates the difficult question of whether disputes related to minority and shareholder rights in India can be resolved using arbitration or whether statutory authorities such as the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) must determine the matter. The paper analyses the framework created by the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the Companies Act, 2013 and the regulatory framework imposed by SEBI. It uses the principles established by several court decisions, notably Booz Allen, Vidya Drolia, and Deccan Paper Mills, to distinguish arbitration of a statutory matter versus arbitration of a contractual dispute. It brings to notice the distinction that the courts have taken a cautious but evolving approach that has recognised the party autonomy in commercial disputes, but concluded that arbitral tribunals do; however, do not have jurisdiction over corporate governance issues, conflicts of interest and public interest matters. It recommends legislative clarity defined upon arbitrability in corporate matters, and focuses on developing a balanced legal framework to improve predictability and extend minority shareholder rights.</jats:p>
title: ARBITRABILITY OF SHAREHOLDER AND MINORITY RIGHTS DISPUTES: Do Indian Courts Trust Arbitral Tribunals

items.abstract: The Concentrate Questions and Answers series offers the best preparation for tackling exam questions and coursework. Each book includes typical questions, suggested answers with commentary, illustrative diagrams, guidance on how to develop your answer, suggestions for further reading, and advice on exams and coursework. This chapter examines the law on minority shareholder remedies, which provide some limited protection or avenues of redress for a shareholder with grievances concerning the actions of the company, directors, or majority shareholders. The chapter explores, in particular: the rule in Foss v Harbottle, derivative claims; personal claims and the issue of reflective loss; the ‘unfair prejudice’ remedy in Companies Act 2006, s. 994; and petitions to wind up the company on the ‘just and equitable’, ground under Insolvency Act 1986, s. 122(1)(g).
title: 7. Minority Shareholder Remedies

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines whether stronger minority shareholder rights affect corporate cash holdings in an emerging-market setting. Using India’s 2015 related-party transaction voting regulation as a quasi-natural experiment, we test whether firms with greater pre-regulation exposure to related-party transactions adjust cash policies after the reform. The regulation restricted interested or dominant shareholders from voting on material related-party transactions, thereby strengthening minority shareholders’ approval rights. Using a firm fixed-effects difference-in-differences design for Indian listed firms from 2011 to 2018, we find that cash holdings decline significantly among firms with high pre-regulation opportunistic related-party transactions. In contrast, firms primarily engaged in business-oriented related-party transactions show no comparable decline. The results are robust to using excess cash as an alternative dependent variable and to entropy-balanced samples. Overall, the evidence suggests that stronger minority shareholder protection reduces agency-driven cash retention by dominant shareholders and constrains the use of cash holdings as a channel for private benefit extraction.</jats:p>
title: Minority Shareholder Rights and Cash Holdings: Evidence from Related-Party Transaction Regulation in India

items.abstract: <jats:p>We examine the relation between minority shareholder protection laws, ownership concentration, and board independence. Minority shareholder rights is a country-level governance variable. Ownership structure and board composition represent firm-level governance variables. Prior research hypothesizes anddocuments a negative relation between countries' minority shareholder rights quality and firms' ownership concentration. We introduce the hypothesis that shareholder protection rights and firms' board independence are positively related. When a country's minority shareholder rights are strong, thenminority shareholders should have the legal power to affect board composition. Using a sample of large firms from 14 European countries, we test both hypotheses and find that countries with stronger shareholder protection rights have firms with lower ownership concentrations and with more independent directors, consistent with both hypotheses. We also find evidence that ownership concentration and board independence are negatively related.</jats:p>
title: Large Shareholders, Board Independence, and Minority Shareholder Rights: Evidence from Europe

<jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Purpose</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – The purpose of this paper is to examine the impact of legal protection of bank minority shareholders (noncontrolling shareholders) and bank creditors (e.g. depositors or debt-holders) on bank dividend payout policies using a panel data set of 5,918 banks from 52 countries over the period 1998-2007, after controlling for country-level deposit insurance coverage and bank- and country-level regulatory pressures. </jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
            <jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – Tobit panel regression models are used to examine the impact of legal protection of shareholders and creditors on bank dividend payout amounts. And, logit panel regression models are used to examine the impact of legal protection of shareholders and creditors on banks’ likelihood to pay dividends. </jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
            <jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Findings</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – The authors support the outcome hypothesis by finding that banks pay higher amount of dividends and, are more likely to pay dividends in strong minority shareholder protection countries. However, the authors reject the substitute hypothesis by finding that banks pay higher dividends and are more likely to pay dividends in weak creditor rights countries, and banks do not substitute weak creditor rights with lower dividend payout amounts. Contrary, the authors support the literature which argues the importance of creditor rights for capital market development because one possible reason for low dividend payouts in strong creditor rights countries could be that the banks retain more profits for extending more loans. </jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
            <jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Practical implications</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – By finding that creditor rights index has a negative relation with bank dividend policies in contrast to its positive relation with nonfinancial firms’ dividend policies, the authors support the literature which argues that managers of banks give less importance to factors such as current degree of financial leverage, the contractual constraints such as dividend restrictions in debt contracts, and the financing considerations such as the cost of raising external funds, while deciding about the dividend payments. The authors also suggest to keep financial and nonfinancial firms separate, to better understand the dividend puzzle. </jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
            <jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Originality/value</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – Extant literature recognizes that legal institutions such as shareholder protection and creditor rights affect corporate firms’ dividend policies significantly but largely excludes banking sector. This paper, by examining the relations between legal protection of shareholders and creditors and bank dividend policies, fills this research gap.</jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
title: Shareholder protection, creditor rights and bank dividend policies

items.abstract:
<jats:p><p><span>This Article explores dividend policy as a mechanism for reducing agency costs rather than merely distributing profits. Because U.S. corporations finance most investment through retained earnings, managers can bypass capital market scrutiny and pursue inefficient or self-serving projects. Courts defer broadly to managerial discretion over dividends, leaving shareholders with limited tools to discipline such behavior.</span></p>
<p><span>The Article proposes a Shareholder Dividend Option: a rule requiring firms to annually offer each shareholder the right to elect a cash or stock dividend equal to their pro rata share of earnings. This individualized mechanism shifts control over earnings retention from managers to shareholders, mitigating agency costs without requiring collective action, such as shareholder vote on dividends.</span></p>
<p><span>The shareholder dividend option is compared to other mechanisms—takeovers and debt—that serve similar disciplining functions. While takeovers are costly and reactive, and debt imposes rigid constraints and introduces its own agency conflicts, the shareholder dividend option offers an ex ante, flexible, and targeted solution.</span></p>
<p><span>A key barrier is tax treatment: current law taxes the entire option as cash, even if reinvested. The Article explores reforms to eliminate this distortion and argues that courts and accounting rules can support implementation. The shareholder dividend option would empower shareholders, enhance market discipline, and improve allocative efficiency in corporate investment.</span></p></jats:p>
title: Shareholder Dividend Options
Is the Separation between Cash Flow and Control Rights a Good Proxy for Minority Shareholder Expropriation?
